traveler: José Antonio de la Sierra (José Antonio de Sierra)
title: The Initial J: the Assayer of Potosí and the First Coinage of the Provincias Unidas
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Potosí, the assayer without a birth record
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: no birth record has been found; the year is obtained by subtracting a stated age of about 67 at his 1813 appointment (Centro Numismático El Patacón, 2009). Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: A man is born somewhere in the Spanish empire in the middle of the eighteenth century and no register keeps the day. What survives of him begins sixty-seven years later, inside this building, and consists of a post, a charge, a verdict, and one letter stamped into metal. No source names his parents, his birthplace, his schooling, or the road that brings him to the mountain. The only reason a year can be written down at all is that a clerk once recorded his age when a government at war handed him an office he was not qualified to hold.
sources: Centro Numismático El Patacón blog, April 2009 (cnbelpatacon.blogspot.com)
Absence of any birth record across billetesargentinos.com.ar, economatos.blogspot.com, BCRA, es.wikipedia
suggested_refs: The Casa Nacional de Moneda de Potosí, the one building in which José Antonio de la Sierra is documented at all

stops.name: Cerro Rico de Potosí, the ore that comes down to the presses
stops.date_confidence: undated: the sources place no year on his relation to the mountain, and no source places him on it at all. The date marks the eve of the wars, not an event.
stops.campa: The mountain stands above the town and has been feeding the presses below it since the sixteenth century. The ore comes down by mule and on the backs of men, is smelted, refined, and brought at last to the crucibles where the fineness of the metal must be sworn to before anything is struck. No source puts Sierra on the slopes. His whole connection to the Cerro runs through the silver itself: it arrives at his furnace as bullion of uncertain purity and leaves his hands as a number that the mint will guarantee.
sources: billetesargentinos.com.ar, 'Primeras Monedas de Potosí'
es.wikipedia, 'Cerro Rico'
suggested_refs: The Cerro Rico de Potosí, source of the silver of the 1813 emission

stops.name: Potosí, the mint abandoned after Huaqui
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; the sources give 1811 without a month for the abandonment of Potosí after Huaqui.
stops.campa: The patriot army is broken at Huaqui and the Argentine forces let go of Potosí and its mint, ending the first occupation of the Villa Imperial. The royal administration returns to the coining rooms and the dies of Ferdinand VII go back on the presses. The officials of the house keep their benches through the change of flag, as officials of that house have kept them through every change of flag for two hundred and fifty years. Sierra is among them, in a subordinate rank, and nobody records what he thinks of any of it.
sources: Instituto Histórico Bicentenario, Poder Legislativo de Corrientes, 'La Primera Moneda Argentina' (PDF)
suggested_refs: The first patriot occupation of the Potosí mint, ended by the defeat at Huaqui in 1811

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the interim founder at the crucibles
stops.date_confidence: attested as prior to 1813 without a start date; the sources say only that he held the post before his promotion.
stops.campa: His post is fundidor interino: interim founder, the man at the furnace who reduces the metal for the assay and the strike. It is a working rank rather than a commission, held on an acting basis by someone the house has never qualified for the office. He is in his sixties. Above him sit the assayers, the chief of the engraving, the treasurer, the Conde who governs the whole establishment for the crown. Nothing in the arrangement suggests that his initial will be the mark on the first coinage of a country that does not yet exist.
sources: Centro Numismático El Patacón blog, April 2009
suggested_refs: The office of fundidor at a Spanish colonial mint, subordinate to the assayer and the talla

segments.name: The Road That Reopens the Villa Imperial

stops.name: Campo de las Carreras, Tucumán, the retreat that is refused
stops.date_confidence: attested; the battle runs 24 to 25 September 1812.
stops.campa: Belgrano disobeys the order to fall back on Córdoba and stands at the Campo de las Carreras outside San Miguel de Tucumán, where he breaks Tristán's royalist army over two days of September. The road north is opened. Between this field and the coining rooms of Potosí lie eight hundred miles, a second battle, and nine months. Every die that Sierra will assay depends on the order disobeyed on this field. At the far end of that road the mint is still striking for Ferdinand VII, and the men at its furnaces do not yet know that anyone is coming for it.
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Batalla de Tucumán'
elarcondelahistoria.com, 'Historia de nuestra moneda (1813)'
suggested_refs: The Campo de las Carreras at San Miguel de Tucumán, 24 to 25 September 1812

stops.name: Campo de Castañares, Salta, the road opened but not the mint
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the plain of Castañares, in the northern zone of Salta, Belgrano takes the royalist army entire and makes Tristán swear not to bear arms again against the Provincias Unidas. The victory does not deliver Potosí; it opens the way to it. Almost three months will pass before patriot troops enter the Villa Imperial, and through those months the men of the mint go on striking coin in the name of Ferdinand VII, not knowing which government will be paying their salaries by winter. The decree that will change the face of that coin has not yet been written in Buenos Aires.
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Batalla de Salta'
es.wikipedia, 'Segunda expedición auxiliadora al Alto Perú'
billetesargentinos.com.ar, 'Primeras Monedas de Potosí'
suggested_refs: Campo Castañares, Salta, 20 February 1813, and the three-month interval before Potosí fell

stops.name: Consulado de Buenos Aires, the Assembly orders new dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate is approximate, since no source consulted geolocates the Consulado building, and the point marks the historic civic block rather than a surveyed address.
stops.campa: The Asamblea General Constituyente, sitting in the building of the Consulado, orders that new dies be opened and engraved at the mint of Potosí: on one face the seal of the Assembly without its sun, on the other a radiant sun and the legend EN UNION Y LIBERTAD. The Assembly has no engraver in the room and no mint of its own. It has a mountain eight hundred miles away, a house of coining still in enemy hands, and whatever officials the retreating royalists will leave behind in it.
sources: Instituto Histórico Bicentenario, 'La Primera Moneda Argentina' (PDF), quoting the decree of 13 April 1813
es.wikipedia, 'Asamblea del Año XIII'
BCRA, 'Bicentenario de la primera moneda patria'
suggested_refs: The decree of 13 April 1813 of the Asamblea del Año XIII, ordering the first national coinage

stops.name: Potosí, the vanguard enters the Villa Imperial
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Eustaquio Díaz Vélez rides into the Villa Imperial at the head of the vanguard and the Casa Real de Moneda changes government for the second time in two years. Behind the royalist withdrawal go the trained officials: engravers, assayers, the men who hold the crown's qualifications. What is left in the coining rooms is a skeleton of subalterns and acting men, and an order coming up the road from Buenos Aires to strike a coinage that nobody in the building has ever seen designed.
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Segunda expedición auxiliadora al Alto Perú'
Centro Numismático El Patacón blog, April 2009
suggested_refs: The entry of Díaz Vélez into Potosí, 7 May 1813, twelve days before Belgrano

stops.name: Casa Real de Moneda, the general takes his headquarters in the mint
stops.date_confidence: attested; Belgrano reaches Potosí on 19 May 1813 and the headquarters in the mint is dated 21 June.
stops.campa: Belgrano establishes his headquarters inside the Casa Real de Moneda itself, so that the general commanding the Army of the North and the officials who will strike the first coinage of the Provincias Unidas are working under one roof. The building is fortress, treasury and government at once: courtyards, furnaces, the great wooden laminating machines, the rooms where the silver of the mountain becomes money. Sierra, sixty-seven years old and holding an interim rank, is somewhere inside it.
sources: belgrano.journey.json, stop 'Potosí, el cuartel general en la Villa Imperial'
BCRA, 'Bicentenario de la primera moneda patria'
suggested_refs: The Casa Real de Moneda de Potosí as Belgrano's headquarters, June 1813

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the officers who fled and the men raised in their place
stops.date_confidence: the sources date the promotions to 1813 without a month; placed here between the patriot occupation and the striking of the coin.
stops.campa: The mint counts what the retreat has taken. Numerous officials have gone north with Goyeneche, and the offices they held must be filled from below, out of a staff the house itself does not consider qualified. Pedro Benavídez, second officer, is raised to Talla Mayor, chief of the engraving. The office of assayer, which certifies the fineness of every piece the house issues, is handed to the interim founder. The war turns a shortage of trained men into a promotion, and the promotion will be held against him.
stops.quote: Numerosos oficiales de la Casa de Moneda huyeron con Goyeneche y por esta razón se debió ascender a oficiales subalternos, muchos de los cuales no estaban suficientemente capacitados pare ejercer los nuevos cargos habiendo cometido numerosos errores. Por ejemplo, el oficial 2do Pedro Venavidez fue promovido a Talla Mayor y el oficio de ensayador se encomendó a un fundidor interino de 67 años, José Antonio de Sierra.
stops.quote_source: Centro Numismático El Patacón, blog post, April 2009, summarising Potosí mint records
sources: Centro Numismático El Patacón blog, April 2009
suggested_refs: The staffing crisis of the Potosí mint after the royalist withdrawal of 1813

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the sala de balanza
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1813 only; no source dates the day he takes up the assayer's office, and no document places him in this particular room.
stops.campa: In the assay and weighing room the fineness of the metal is settled before anything is struck: samples cupelled, weights compared, a figure sworn to and written down. Out of this room goes the mint's word about its own silver, to whoever will take the coin. The office is given to José Antonio de Sierra at sixty-seven, on an emergency, without the qualification the crown would have demanded in peacetime. No document places him in this chamber; the division of labour in a colonial mint places him there.
stops.quote: El oficio de ensayador se encomendó a José Antonio de Sierra.
sources: economatos.blogspot.com, 'Monedas Patrias'
billetesargentinos.com.ar, 'Primeras Monedas de Potosí'
Reconstruction from the standard operating structure of a colonial mint
suggested_refs: The sala de balanza of the Potosí mint, where fineness was certified before striking

stops.name: Fortaleza de Buenos Aires, the Executive promulgates the coin
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: From the Fortaleza the Executive Power promulgates the Assembly's decree and orders the new coin into circulation at the same weight and fineness as the Spanish money it replaces. Antonio Álvarez de Jonte, José Julián Pérez and Nicolás Rodríguez Peña sign it, with Manuel José García as secretary. The intrinsic value is not to change; only the face is. A merchant is to take the sun and the shield exactly as he took the king, and it is the assayer at Potosí who has to make that promise true in metal.
sources: Instituto Histórico Bicentenario, 'La Primera Moneda Argentina' (PDF)
suggested_refs: The promulgation of 28 July 1813 from the Fortaleza de Buenos Aires, signed by the Segundo Triunvirato

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the legends come out reversed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the sources say the coin was circulating within days of the promulgation but give no exact date for the first strike.
stops.campa: The dies are opened at Potosí and the coin is in hand within days. What comes off the presses is not quite what Buenos Aires ordered: the shield with EN UNION Y LIBERTAD stands on one face and the radiant sun with PROVINCIAS DEL RIO DE LA PLATA on the other, the two legends exchanged from the wording of the decree. Eight hundred miles of road separate the decree from the burin, and the burin has the last word on the metal. What comes out of the press is not what the Assembly described, and it goes into circulation anyway.
sources: Instituto Histórico Bicentenario, 'La Primera Moneda Argentina' (PDF)
suggested_refs: The 1813 Potosí dies, whose legends invert the arrangement prescribed by the decree of 13 April

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the eight reales in silver
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1813; individual denominations are not separately dated in the sources.
stops.campa: The eight reales comes off the press at the weight and fineness of the Spanish piece it replaces, marked PTS in monogram for the house and J for the man who has sworn to the metal. It is the coin the mule trains carry, the coin the mining camps are paid in, the coin that will turn up a century later in cash hoards from Lima to Manila. Nothing on it names the assayer. The single letter stands in for a name that no register of birth or death anywhere records.
stops.quote: Provincias Unidas del Río de la Plata. 8 Reales 1813 J (José Antonio de Sierra) Casa de Moneda de Potosí.
stops.quote_source: Río de La Plata numismatics blog, 'Selección de piezas Potosinas' (rpnumis.com)
sources: rpnumis.com, 'Selección de piezas Potosinas'
elarcondelahistoria.com, 'Historia de nuestra moneda (1813)'
Numista, 1813 Provincias del Río de la Plata, silver series at .896 fine

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the gold escudos
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1813; the gold strike is not separately dated in the sources.
stops.campa: Gold follows the silver: one, two, four and eight escudos at eight hundred and seventy five thousandths fine, the eight-escudo piece twenty seven grams and thirty five millimetres across, carrying the sun, military trophies where the silver carries the shield, and the same assayer's J. Very few are struck and fewer survive. Two centuries on, one of these pieces will sell for more than any other Argentine coin ever has, and the provenance will run back through the auction catalogue to the letter Sierra put on the metal.
sources: Numista, 1813 Provincias del Río de la Plata, KM#6-9, gold at .875 fine
Infobae, 'La increíble historia de 8 Escudos' (2021)
Instituto Histórico Bicentenario, 'La Primera Moneda Argentina' (PDF)
suggested_refs: The 1813 Potosí gold escudos, 1, 2, 4 and 8, all bearing the assayer's J

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the small change of the revolution
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1813; the minor denominations are not separately dated in the sources.
stops.campa: Beneath the great pieces runs the ordinary money: half, one, two and four reales in silver, one, two and four escudos in gold, every one of them assayed under the same mark. This is the coinage that actually circulates, the change of a country at war paying for mules and maize and powder with the sun of a revolution stamped on it. Of the two-escudo pieces, one museum account holds that only two are now known to survive; no other source that could be reached repeats the figure.
sources: Google Arts & Culture, Museo Histórico y Numismático Héctor Carlos Janson, 'Primeras monedas patrias'
Numista, 1813 Provincias del Río de la Plata series
elarcondelahistoria.com, 'Historia de nuestra moneda (1813)'

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, twenty varieties of a single coin
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1813; the varieties are catalogued by later numismatists, not dated individually.
stops.campa: Matrices, punches and trained hands are all short, and it shows in the metal. The eight-real piece of this single year survives in at least twenty documented varieties, differing in the count and set of the sun's rays, in the placing of letters, in the position of a numeral. Legends come out crowded and misspelled, a letter missing where the burin ran out of room. The dies are cut by men who have held their offices a few weeks, in a house that has lost the engravers who trained them, and each one comes out of the shop a little different from the last.
sources: Instituto Histórico Bicentenario, 'La Primera Moneda Argentina' (PDF)
Google Arts & Culture, Museo Histórico y Numismático Héctor Carlos Janson
suggested_refs: The catalogued die varieties of the 1813 Potosí 8 reales

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the initial J
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1813, which is the whole span in which his mark appears.
stops.campa: The mark of a colonial mint is a signature and a guarantee at once: the house identifies itself, the assayer identifies himself, and if the fineness comes up short it is the assayer who answers for it. PTS names the Villa Imperial. J names José Antonio de Sierra. Every piece of gold and silver struck at Potosí for the Provincias Unidas del Río de la Plata in 1813 carries that letter, from the half real up to the eight escudos. Nothing else he signed has been found in any archive or any catalogue.
stops.quote: La inicial J. corresponde al ensayador José Antonio de Sierra.
stops.quote_source: Billetes Argentinos, 'Primeras Monedas de Potosí' (billetesargentinos.com.ar); the same sentence appears verbatim at economatos.blogspot.com
sources: billetesargentinos.com.ar, 'Primeras Monedas de Potosí'
economatos.blogspot.com, 'Monedas Patrias'
Centro Numismático El Patacón blog, April 2009
suggested_refs: The assay marks of the Potosí mint, PTS monogram and assayer's initial

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, who designed it and who cut the dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1813; the dispute over authorship is not itself datable.
stops.campa: The sources do not agree about who made this coin. Popular accounts say Sierra designed it. The specialist numismatic literature calls him strictly the assayer and gives the cutting of the dies to Pedro Benavídez, chief of the engraving. A third line credits the shield and the sun to Juan de Dios Rivera, the engraver from Cusco commissioned by the deputy Agustín Donado, while the Spanish record of the national arms states that no conclusive evidence of the design's authorship exists. What is documented of Sierra is one office and one letter.
stops.quote: La misma fue diseñadas por José Antonio de Sierra y producida en la ciudad de Potosí, que por el año 1813 cayó bajo el control del Ejercito Libertador Patriota liderado por el General Manuel Belgrano.
stops.quote_source: Infobae, 'La increíble historia de 8 Escudos, la moneda más cara de Argentina', 25 September 2021
sources: Infobae, 25 September 2021
Instituto Histórico Bicentenario, 'La Primera Moneda Argentina' (PDF), naming Pedro Benavídez

stops.name: Vilcapugio, the day that turns in the afternoon
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Belgrano meets Pezuela on the plain of Vilcapugio and the day goes against him. He loses his artillery and a third of his army in a battle that had looked won by the afternoon. The road that opened at Tucumán and Salta begins to close in the other direction. In the coining rooms of Potosí the presses are still running, striking sun and shield for a government whose army in Upper Peru has just been cut in half, and the men working them have five weeks left.
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Batalla de Vilcapugio'
billetesargentinos.com.ar, 'Primeras Monedas de Potosí'
suggested_refs: The field of Vilcapugio, 1 October 1813

stops.name: Ayohuma, the Army of the North destroyed
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the llanos of Ayohuma what remains of the Army of the North is broken. Belgrano loses his guns, his ammunition and the last force capable of holding Upper Peru; what walks south afterwards cannot defend a city. The patriot hold on Potosí, on the mountain and on the mint at its foot, has six days to live. The first coinage of the Provincias Unidas turns out to be the coinage of a single season, and the season ends here, seven hundred kilometres from the room that ordered it.
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Batalla de Ayohuma'
elarcondelahistoria.com, 'Historia de nuestra moneda (1813)'
suggested_refs: The llanos de Ayohuma, partido de Chayanta, 14 November 1813

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the powder laid under the mint
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of the evacuation; belgrano.journey.json dates the mining of the building to September 1813, which is left standing as a discrepancy rather than adjudicated.
stops.campa: Evacuating the Villa Imperial before Pezuela's advance, Belgrano orders the Casa de Moneda mined and blown up rather than left to the crown. The powder is laid. The order is not carried out: tradition holds the fuse was cut, and the building survives entire, presses, furnaces, assay room and all. The general who made his headquarters here in June leaves it standing for the enemy in November, and the officials who struck coin for him stay behind in the rooms he had meant to destroy.
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Segunda expedición auxiliadora al Alto Perú'
belgrano.journey.json, stop 'Potosí, la mina bajo la Casa de Moneda'
suggested_refs: The order to blow up the Casa de Moneda de Potosí, November 1813, and the cut fuse

stops.name: Potosí, the royalists re-enter
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The royalist army enters Potosí the day after the patriots leave. The dies of the sun are put away and the dies of Ferdinand VII come back out, and the men of the mint, who have now served three governments in two years without moving from their benches, are looked over one at a time to establish what each of them did while the insurgents held the town. Of everyone in the building, the one with an initial stamped on hundreds of thousands of coins is the least able to argue that the question does not apply to him.
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Segunda expedición auxiliadora al Alto Perú'
elarcondelahistoria.com, 'Historia de nuestra moneda (1813)'
suggested_refs: The royalist reoccupation of Potosí, 20 November 1813

stops.name: Potosí, arrested as a collaborator
stops.date_confidence: the sources give only 1813 or 1814 for the arrest; the date here is placed immediately after the royalist reoccupation and is not attested to the day.
stops.campa: He is arrested as a collaborator. The charge is infidencia, disloyalty to the king, and the evidence against him is the coinage itself: he certified the metal of a money struck to replace the crown's face, and his letter is on all of it. That he was sixty-seven and holding an acting rank when the patriot government handed him the office does not appear to weigh in the first instance. The mint's qualified assayers had left with Goyeneche. The man who took their bench is the man still available.
stops.quote: El fundidor José Antonio de Sierra, cuya inicial "J" aparece en todas las monedas para las Provincias Unidas del Río de la Plata de 1813, fue detenido por colaboracionista y permaneció en prisión por mas de un año hasta el 25 de enero de 1815, cuando el Conde de la Casa de Real de Moneda dictamino su inocencia y lo repuso en su antiguo empleo.
stops.quote_source: Centro Numismático El Patacón, blog post, April 2009
sources: Centro Numismático El Patacón blog, April 2009, the single source for the arrest
suggested_refs: The infidencia proceedings at Potosí after the royalist reoccupation of November 1813

stops.name: Potosí, more than a year in prison
stops.date_confidence: attested only as a duration of more than a year ending 25 January 1815; the midpoint is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He stays in prison more than a year. Around him the war goes back and forth over the mountain; the coin he assayed keeps circulating in both directions, taken in royalist Potosí and in patriot Salta alike because the silver in it is good, which is the one thing he was responsible for and the one thing nobody disputes. No source records where he is held, on what allowance, or whether his household is with him. Only the length of it is written down, and the date on which it ends.
sources: Centro Numismático El Patacón blog, April 2009
Absence of any custodial record in the sources consulted
suggested_refs: The Potosí gaol and the infidencia detentions of 1814

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the verdict of the Conde
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Conde de la Real Casa de Moneda rules that Don José Antonio Sierra has purified his conduct: that everything charged against him was the effect of fear before the armed force of the government of the Río de la Plata, that he had no liberty to refuse the orders of the intruding officials, and that he stands free of the crime of infidencia against the king, in his good repute and fame as he stood before the insurgents entered this Villa. He is restored to his former employment. It is the longest document about him that exists.
stops.quote: Autos y vistos... se declare que Don José Antonio Sierra ha purificado su conducta de los hechos de que ha sido acusado y que todos fueron efecto del temor por la fuerza de las armas del gobierno del Río de la Plata, sin que en aquellas circunstancias tuviese libertad de repulsar las ordenes de los mandarines intrusos y en su virtud, libre de delito de infidencia contra el rey, quedando en su buena reputación y fama como lo estuvo antes de entrar los insurgentes en esta Villa.
stops.quote_source: Fallo of the Conde de la Casa de la Real de Moneda de Potosí, 25 January 1815, as reproduced by the Centro Numismático El Patacón blog
sources: Centro Numismático El Patacón blog, April 2009, quoting the verdict
suggested_refs: The fallo of 25 January 1815 absolving Sierra of infidencia

stops.name: Potosí, the third expedition takes the town
stops.date_confidence: attested; the vanguard enters 1 May 1815 and Rondeau on 9 May.
stops.campa: A third patriot expedition comes up into Upper Peru and Rondeau's men take Potosí again. The Assembly's coin can be struck again; the mountain and the house are back in the hands of the government whose money Sierra marked twenty months earlier. He is in the town, exonerated by a royal court, restored to his old employment, four months out of a cell, and the one man in Potosí who has already done this exact work for this exact government. The one thing the returning administration will not do is put him back on the assayer's bench.
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Tercera expedición auxiliadora al Alto Perú'
billetesargentinos.com.ar, 'Primeras Monedas de Potosí'
suggested_refs: Rondeau's occupation of Potosí, May to December 1815

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the man they cannot count on
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1815 occupation without a month; placed after Rondeau's entry and before the August appointments.
stops.campa: They cannot count on Sierra, who had acted in 1813. It is the last thing the record says about him while he is alive and it can be read two ways: a man who will not put his letter on patriot silver a second time after a year in a cell for the first, or a man the patriots no longer trust because a royal court has just certified that he served them out of fear. Neither reading is written down anywhere, in any source that survives, and the sentence is the whole of the evidence. The office goes to somebody else, and the second emission of the Villa Imperial is marked with another man's letter.
stops.quote: pues no se pudo contar con Sierra, que había actuado en 1813
sources: economatos.blogspot.com, 'Monedas Patrias'
billetesargentinos.com.ar, 'Primeras Monedas de Potosí'
suggested_refs: The 1815 Potosí emission and the assayers appointed in Sierra's place

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, the letter F replaces the letter J
stops.date_confidence: contested: the sources give both 30 and 31 August 1815 for the Matos appointment and neither could be verified; 30 August is used here and the discrepancy is left standing.
stops.campa: Francisco José de Matos is appointed first assayer of the Potosí mint and the silver of the second emission goes out marked F. Leandro Ozio is named second assayer beside him. One account puts an Isidro Escarza in the office before Matos, and it cannot be corroborated anywhere else. The second emission is silver only, struck by improvised hands, and the mint's own papers as later numismatists read them report the metal coming out short of the standard the first emission had held.
sources: elarcondelahistoria.com, 'Historia de la Moneda Argentina (1813)'

stops.name: Viluma, the last patriot army in Upper Peru
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Rondeau's army is destroyed on the field of Viluma, near Sipe Sipe, by Pezuela. It is the last attempt of the Provincias Unidas to hold Upper Peru; after this the frontier settles on the Salta highlands and stays there, and the mountain that funded three centuries of empire passes out of Argentine history. The coin with the sun on it goes on circulating for decades, long after the country that struck it has stopped being able to reach the place where it was made.

stops.name: Potosí, the town lost for good
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Potosí is lost on the sixteenth of December and does not change hands again in the war of independence. Whatever remains of the patriot administration of the mint goes south with the wreck of the army. The house returns to striking for Ferdinand VII and will keep striking for him until Ayacucho settles the question nine years later. Sierra, if he is still at a bench under the restored crown, works there without any source noticing him, and the coinage he assayed becomes a thing that circulates in a country his mint no longer belongs to.

stops.name: Casa de la Moneda de Potosí, where the record stops
stops.date_confidence: no source consulted records a death date, a place of death, or any employment after 1815; the date is a placeholder marking the end of the documentary record, not an event.
stops.campa: After the verdict of January and the sentence about not being able to count on him, nothing. No death date, no burial, no parish entry, no pension, no further appointment, no mention in any mint list that could be located. A namesake appears in a database as a Peruvian politician of the same century, with no dates and no connection to the mint, and is very likely a different man. His documented life runs two years and consists entirely of what he did to metal.

stops.name: Pampa de la Quinua, Ayacucho, the last royal coinage ends
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The royalist army is broken on the pampa of La Quinua and Spanish rule in South America ends. Within months the Villa Imperial stops striking coin in the name of Ferdinand VII, and the house that Sierra worked in passes to the new republic of Bolivia. Every government whose money he handled is by now gone: the crown that tried him, the Provincias Unidas he was tried for serving, and the viceroyalty that had qualified the assayers he was promoted to replace.

stops.name: Ira and Larry Goldberg auction rooms, the Colección Millenia sale
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the venue is unconfirmed, since the single source reporting the sale names the auction firm but no city, and the coordinate marks the firm's own Los Angeles offices.
stops.campa: An 1813 Potosí eight escudos, authenticated by the Argentine numismatists Héctor Carlos Janson and Alberto Derman, is sold in the Colección Millenia sale held by the auctioneers Ira and Larry Goldberg for one hundred and sixty one thousand dollars, the highest price ever paid for an Argentine coin. The catalogue describes the sun, the trophies, the mint monogram and the assayer's initial. When a Buenos Aires newspaper retells the sale thirteen years later, it names Sierra as the man who designed the coin, a claim the numismatic literature does not support.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the coinage in the Museo Janson
stops.date_confidence: undated: the museum's custody is continuous and no source dates the acquisition; the year is a placeholder for the present.
stops.campa: Two blocks from the Plaza de Mayo the Central Bank keeps the coinage of 1813: the gold escudos, the silver reales, the misstruck legends, the varieties of the sun, laid out in cases under glass. The pieces are shown as the first money of the country, and the labels name the Assembly, the decree, the mint at Potosí, the general whose army held it. The man whose office was to guarantee that the metal in them was what it claimed to be is present in the case as a single letter, repeated on every piece, unexplained.

stops.name: Casa Nacional de Moneda, Potosí, the building still standing
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the Andean Parliament recognition; the ownership arrangement is current as reported.
stops.campa: The building still stands over Potosí, its ownership split between the Bolivian judiciary and the municipality, its transfer to a cultural foundation under negotiation, its standing as regional heritage recognised by the Andean Parliament. Visitors are shown the furnaces, the wooden laminating machines, the room where metal was weighed and certified. There is no monument to Sierra inside it and none anywhere else: no statue, no plaque, no grave. What commemorates him is the letter on a few thousand surviving coins.
